subject: How do I check unidimensionality in a 3PL using survey.weights

messages.author: fd1c548a0ef4b2ee
messages.subject: How do I check unidimensionality in a 3PL using survey.weights
parts:
Hello,
I'm a PhD student in veterinary epidemiology.
My thesis is about evaluating farm biosecurity practices.
We will work with IRT to evaluate the ability of each property to adopt these practices.
We have a survey applied to 604 farms with sampling weights.
I found your package looking for IRT with sampling weights.

I would like to know if there is a function or a guideline to check for unidimensionality? 
At these moment I used psych :: fa.parallel, as you recommended in previous topic.
The result was "Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors = 5 and the number of components = 4"

Or how is the best way or criteria to exclude some variables that be interfering in unidimensionality?

Or if is more plausible to work with an multidimensional model?

Thanks
Gustavo

On Wed, Jul 19, 2017 at 1:57 PM, Gustavo Silva <gustav...@hotmail.com> wrote:
Hello,
I'm a PhD student in veterinary epidemiology.
My thesis is about evaluating farm biosecurity practices.
We will work with IRT to evaluate the ability of each property to adopt these practices.
We have a survey applied to 604 farms with sampling weights.
I found your package looking for IRT with sampling weights.

I would like to know if there is a function or a guideline to check for unidimensionality? 
At these moment I used psych :: fa.parallel, as you recommended in previous topic.
The result was "Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors = 5 and the number of components = 4"

This works well provided that the data are reasonably continuous, otherwise you'll want psych::fa.parallel.poly() instead for categorical data. Checking dimensionality is difficult in IRT models due to the curse of dimensionality, though you could compare models using the anova() function and using a more optimal estimation algorithm than strict quadrature (e.g., MHRM, quasi-monte carlo, etc).

Or how is the best way or criteria to exclude some variables that be interfering in unidimensionality?

Or if is more plausible to work with an multidimensional model?

Given the number of variables you have multidimensional is likely. I would probably recommend sticking to approximate methods provided by the factor analysis tradition than move into more confirmatory methods found in IRT.
 

Thanks
Gustavo

Hi,

Anyone don't know how to discover the optimal number of factors in item factor analysis perspectives especially 'model based approach'.

Currently, I'm using DIC information. Extract a factor, and differ with the two-factor model. if the two-factor model fits well than one factor, I take the two-factor model.
After that, I extract one more factor; the three-factor model. Do this work "repeat iteratively" until finding "global optimal number of the factor".

I made these actions "to use very personally" with the command; source('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seonghobae/k.aefa/master/k.aefa3.R')
This source referenced from Preacher, Zhang, Kim, & Meis (2013) work, and will install so much package what related with psychometrics, sorry to inconvenience.

Preacher, K. J., Zhang, G., Kim, C., & Mels, G. (2013). Choosing the optimal number of factors in exploratory factor analysis: A model selection perspective. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 48(1), 28-56.

After loading that source, you may check the number of factors iteratively. 

mod1 <- deepFA(fastFIFA(your_data_frame, survey.weights = your_survey_weights_vector)) # very experimental code to find the optimal number of factor with survey.weights what import mirt() function

But I agree with Phil. 

Seongho
